topic.name: Double Integrals Over Type I Regions

question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_{-2}^1\int_{e^x}^e \dfrac{x\ln y}{y}\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx &= \int_{-2}^1 x \left[\int_{e^x}^e \dfrac{\ln y}{y}\,\mathrm dy \right]\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^1 x \left[ \dfrac{\ln^2 y}{2} \right]_{e^x}^e \,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\int_{-2}^1 x \left(\dfrac{\ln ^2 e}{2}-\dfrac{\ln^2 e^x}{2} \right) \,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\int_{-2}^1 x \left(\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) \,\mathrm dx \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_{-2}^1 x \left(\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right) \,\mathrm dx &= \int_{-2}^1 \left(\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{2}\right) \,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}- \dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_{-2}^1 \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{4} -\dfrac{(-2)^2}{2}+ \dfrac{(-2)^4}{4}\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}- \dfrac{1}{4}-2+4 \right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{2-1-8+16}{4} \right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{9}{8} \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Repeated Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.explanation:
The integral is defined over the type I region $D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1\le x\le 2, \: \dfrac{1}{x}\le y \le \dfrac{3}{x}\right\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{D}\dfrac{2}{1+4x^2 y^2}\,\mathrm dA&=\int_1^2\int_{1/x}^{3/x} \dfrac{2}{1+4x^2y^2}\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx \end{align*}

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_1^2 \int_{1/x}^{3/x} \dfrac{2}{1+4x^2y^2}\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dx &= \int_1^2 \left[\int_{1/x}^{3/x} \dfrac{2}{1+(2xy)^2}\,\mathrm dy\right]\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\int_1^2\left[\dfrac{1}{x}\arctan (2xy)\right]_{1/x}^{3/x}\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=\int_1^2 \dfrac{1}{x} ( \arctan (6)- \arctan (2) )\,\mathrm dx \\[5pt] &=( \arctan (6)- \arctan (2)) \int_1^2 \dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathrm dx \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} (\arctan (6)- \arctan (2)) \int_1^2 \dfrac{1}{x}\,\mathrm dx &=( \arctan (6)- \arctan (2))\Big[\ln{x}\Big]_1^2 \\[5pt] &=(\arctan (6)- \arctan (2))\cdot(\ln{2}-\ln{1}) \\[5pt] &=(\arctan (6)- \arctan (2)) \ln{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type I Region

question.text: If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines $y=e,$ $x=0,$ and the curve $y=e^x,$ as shown above, then $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \ln(x+y) \, \mathrm{d}A =$
question.explanation:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type I region.

  • To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} e^x &= e \\[3pt] x &= 1 \end{align*} So, $x$-limits are $ 0 \le x \le 1. $

  • To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, we get

\[ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad e^x \leq y \leq e \big\}. \]

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_D \ln(x+y) \,\mathrm{d}A &=\int_0^1 \int_{e^x}^{e} \ln(x+y) \, \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

example.title: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Not Given

question.text: If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the curves $y = 2-x$ and $y = 4-x^2,$ then $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}A =$
question.explanation:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

Now, let's represent $D$ as a type I region.

  • To determine the $x$-limits, we need to find the $x$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $x\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 2 - x &= 4 - x^2\\[5pt] x^2 - x - 2 & = 0\\[5pt] (x-2)(x+1) & = 0 \end{align*} So, $x$-limits are $ -1 \le x \le 2. $

  • To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

As a result, we get

\[ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -1 \leq x \leq 2, \quad 2-x \leq y \leq 4-x^2 \big\}. \]

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows: \begin{align*} \iint\limits_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A &=\int_{-1}^2 \int_{2-x}^{4-x^2} f(x,y) \ \mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_{-1}^2 \left[ \int_{2-x}^{4-x^2} f(x,y) \ \mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

example.title: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Not Given

question.explanation:
The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align*} \int_0^{1}\int_{0}^{3x} x^2 \,\mathrm{d}y \: \mathrm{d}x &= \int_0^{1} x^2 \left[ \int_{0}^{3x} \,\mathrm{d}y \right] \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{1} x^2 \big[\, y \, \big]_{0}^{3x} \, \mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{1} x^2 \big(3x -0 \big) \,\mathrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{1 } 3x^3 \,\mathrm{d}x \end{align*}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \int_0^{1} 3x^3 \,\mathrm{d}x &= \left[\dfrac{3x^4}{4}\right]_0^{1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3(1)^4}{4} - 0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{align*}
